parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the shape of a black-body spectrum - what happens to the position of the peak when a star gets hotter and bluer?
Hint 2: Remember to define both quantities precisely: which temperature is involved, and which special wavelength on the curve is involved, and how they are linked by an inverse proportion.
parts.proper_answer: The thermodynamic temperature $T$ of the surface of a star is inversely proportional to the wavelength $\lambda_{max}$ at which the rate of emission of radiation is maximum. $\lambda_{max}T = \text{constant}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture a black-body curve**
Think of yourself plotting emission rate $P$ against wavelength $\lambda$ for a hot star. It rises to a peak then falls. A hotter star not only emits more at every wavelength, its whole peak shifts to shorter, bluer wavelengths.

Step 2: **State the inverse law precisely**
You can say this in words as: $$T \propto \frac{1}{\lambda_{max}}$$ where $T$ is the thermodynamic (Kelvin) temperature of the star's surface, and $\lambda_{max}$ is the wavelength of maximum emission rate. In equation form: $$\lambda_{max}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K}$$ That constant form earns full credit.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: inverse-square law F = L / (4 pi d^2)
Stefan-Boltzmann law L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4
hints: Hint 1: Compare the two peaks in Fig. 9.2 - which star peaks at shorter wavelength, and what does Wien's law tell you about its surface temperature relative to the Sun at 5770 K?
Hint 2: Look at Fig. 9.1 - it is a straight line of $F$ against $1/d^2$. What does the gradient represent if $F = L/(4\pi d^2)$?
Hint 3: Once you have $L$ and $T$ for star X, which law links luminosity to radius and temperature, allowing you to find $r$?
parts.proper_answer: 1. $(T_X \approx 7000\text{ K})$ star X is hotter than the Sun, $\lambda_{max}$ is shorter. 2. Star X is more luminous than the Sun, $L_X \approx 2.7 \times 10^{27}\text{ W}$ from gradient of Fig. 9.1. 3. Radius of star X $\approx 1.3 \times 10^9\text{ m}$, larger than the Sun.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get temperature from Fig. 9.2**
From Wien's law, shorter $\lambda_{max}$ means higher $T$. Star X peaks at $\lambda \approx 4.1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$, the Sun at $\lambda \approx 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$. So star X is hotter. Using ratios: $$\frac{T_X}{T_{Sun}} = \frac{\lambda_{Sun}}{\lambda_X}$$ With $T_{Sun} = 5770\text{ K}$ this gives $T_X \approx 7000\text{ K}$.

Step 2: **Get luminosity from Fig. 9.1**
Radiant flux intensity obeys: $$F = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}$$ So a plot of $F$ against $d^{-2}$ has gradient $= L/4\pi$. Take a point, e.g. $F \approx 4.2 \times 10^3\text{ W m}^{-2}$ at $d^{-2} = 2.0 \times 10^{-23}\text{ m}^{-2}$: $$\text{gradient} \approx 2.1 \times 10^{26}\text{ W}$$ $$L_X = 4\pi \times \text{gradient} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{27}\text{ W}$$ This is about 7 times the solar luminosity ($3.8 \times 10^{26}\text{ W}$), so star X has higher luminosity.

Step 3: **Get radius from Stefan-Boltzmann law**
Treat star as black body: $$L = 4\pi r^2 \sigma T^4$$ Rearranged: $$r = \sqrt{\frac{L}{4\pi \sigma T^4}}$$ Put $L_X \approx 2.7 \times 10^{27}\text{ W}$, $T_X \approx 7000\text{ K}$, $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}$: $$r_X \approx 1.3 \times 10^9\text{ m}$$ Any three of: higher $T$, $T \approx 7000\text{ K}$, higher $L$, $L$ value, $r$ value are valid conclusions.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: If the whole galaxy is receding from Earth, what happens to the wavelength of light travelling toward us?
Hint 2: If every wavelength is stretched to a longer value, where will the peak of the $P$ against $\lambda$ curve in Fig. 9.2 now appear?
parts.proper_answer: Light from star X is redshifted due to recession. Observed wavelengths are increased, so the peak of maximum emission is shifted to greater wavelength.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall recession means redshift**
A galaxy moving away stretches the light waves in transit. Observed wavelength $\lambda_{obs}$ is greater than emitted wavelength $\lambda_{emit}$. This is cosmological redshift.

Step 2: **Apply to the whole spectrum**
The entire $P$ against $\lambda$ curve is shifted to the right. In particular the wavelength of peak emission rate $\lambda_{max}$ measured on Earth would appear greater than the true emitted value shown in Fig. 9.2.
